relevance_rank_note: A structural NMR study of the microenvironment of the LDL receptor-binding region of the apoE isoforms; its only H4-relevant content is the APOE4-equals-APOE3 LDL receptor affinity null, and the lysine pKa and ferricyanide exposure measurements are charge and solvent-exposure mechanism readouts whose stated binding consequence for apoE4 versus apoE3 is no change.

description: In DMPC phospholipid complexes the 22-kDa amino-terminal fragments of apoE3 and apoE4 bound the LDL receptor with the same affinity as each other and about 100-fold better than apoE2, so the isoform difference that matters for LDL receptor adhesion lies at position 158 and not at the position 112 residue that distinguishes apoE4 from apoE3.
quote: When present in dimyristoyl phosphatidylcholine (DMPC) complexes, the 22-kDa aminoterminal fragments (residues 1–191) of apoE3 and apoE4 bound to the LDLR with ~100-fold greater affinity than the 22-kDa fragment of apoE2.
summary: (APOE3 -> APOE4) -> (no change in LDL receptor binding affinity)
system: Cell-free and cultured-fibroblast binding of recombinant 22-kDa amino-terminal fragments (residues 1-191) of human apoE2, apoE3 and apoE4 expressed in E. coli and reconstituted into discoidal complexes with dimyristoyl phosphatidylcholine at a 3.2:1 lipid-to-protein weight ratio, hydrodynamic diameter about 16 nm and apoE alpha-helical content 65-70 percent; LDL receptor affinity assessed by a fibroblast competitive binding assay against 125I-labelled LDL, with the lipid-free versus DMPC-complexed apoE3 competition concentrations given as 7,000 and 0.7 nM.
location: Abstract and Results (Fig 1A text, 22-kDa apoE3 fibroblast competition), with Discussion 'Role of the C112R mutation'
human_check: No figure image was viewed for this paper; nothing was read off a panel. Against: true, an APOE4-equals-APOE3 null for LDL receptor adhesion, which is the direction opposite to H4. IMPORTANT PROVENANCE CAVEAT the human must weigh: this paper does not itself run an apoE4-versus-apoE3 binding titration. The apoE4-equals-apoE3 affinity statement is carried in the paper's own voice in several places but cited to reference 4 ('ApoE4 binds to the LDLR with the same affinity as apoE3 (4)'; 'When complexed with DMPC, full-length apoE3 and apoE4 and their 22-kDa fragments have the same affinity for the LDLR (4, 34)'; 'this isoform binds as well as apoE3 to the LDLR'; 'the presence of a positive charge at position 112 in apoE4 does not alter LDLR-binding affinity (4)'). The quoted abstract sentence is the one place the comparison is stated without an inline citation, which is why it is the quote here; the human may prefer to treat this row as an asserted literature value rather than a measurement made in this paper, and to downgrade strength accordingly. The only binding number printed for work done here is the apoE3 fibroblast competition concentration pair 7,000 nM (lipid-free) versus 0.7 nM (DMPC-complexed), which is a lipid-state contrast, not an isoform contrast. Effect is qualitative: the ~100-fold figure printed is apoE3-or-apoE4 versus apoE2, not apoE4 versus apoE3, and the apoE4-versus-apoE3 contrast has no magnitude because it is a stated equality. No P and no n are printed for any isoform binding comparison. The Table 1 lysine pKa values (K143 9.5 in apoE3 versus 9.9 in apoE4, a 0.4 pH unit rise; K146 9.2 versus 9.4) and the Table 2 ferricyanide relative downfield shifts (K143 0.95 in both apoE3 and apoE4; K146 1.25 versus 1.18) are deliberately NOT filed as separate H4 findings: the authors state explicitly that the K143 pKa change 'did not alter LDLR-binding affinity' and that the cysteine-arginine interchanges 'did not significantly affect the exposure of any of the lysines to the aqueous phase', so each measurement's stated apoE4-versus-apoE3 binding consequence is the same null already recorded in this row, and filing them separately would multiply one null into three. No pH-dependence of apoE-receptor binding was measured: the pH titrations are of lysine side chains in the protein, not of receptor adhesion, so this paper says nothing about endosomal-pH dissociation.
